entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A short-lived glowing sphere seen during thunderstorms, distinct from ordinary lightning bolts, whose physical cause is still unexplained. It typically lasts only seconds, can move, hover, pass through walls or glass, and vanish with or without an explosion.
entries.background: The term was coined by French scientist François Arago in 1837 and has since generated thousands of eyewitness reports but almost no instrumental recordings, leaving its cause disputed among physicists.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: A description of ball lightning research as a scattered, uncoordinated field where different researchers collect data, build theories, or run lab experiments without a shared framework tying the work together.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.senseHere: A US network of cameras that photographed the night sky continuously for over a decade to track meteors, whose archive was searched for accidental ball lightning images, yielding only two probable captures out of thousands of photographs.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: The Austrian network of sensors that detects and records the location, timing, and electrical strength of lightning strokes across the country, used here to cross-check ball lightning sighting reports against real lightning data.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: The German equivalent network that detects and logs lightning strikes, used in the piece to confirm a nearby lightning stroke coincided with a reported ball lightning sighting.

entries.name: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa
entries.background: A Soviet physicist and Nobel laureate known for work in low-temperature physics, who proposed a theoretical explanation for how ball lightning might be sustained by microwave radiation, though he himself never reported witnessing it.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: A 19th-century Austrian geologist and mineralogist who was a member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna. His detailed 1868 report and sketch of a ball lightning sighting, along with corroborating sightings elsewhere in Vienna, is one of the earliest scientifically documented cases.

entries.name: angular diameter
entries.senseHere: The apparent size of an object in the sky or field of view, measured as an angle rather than an actual physical width, used by observers to estimate how large or how far away a ball lightning object was.

entries.name: Axel Wittmann
entries.background: An astrophysicist at the Göttingen university observatory who, as a child in 1951, witnessed a dramatic ball lightning event that broke into smaller spheres, later publishing a detailed scientific account and calculation of the plasma's energy density.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: An American paleontology professor at Yale University and president of the US National Academy of Sciences, known for his work on dinosaur fossils. He later wrote a detailed account to the journal Nature describing a ball lightning strike aboard a yacht in 1878.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: A German physics professor famous for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrating that electron spin is quantized. He personally witnessed and mathematically analyzed a ball lightning event at Tübingen in 1927, calculating an extremely high travel speed for the object.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: A British radio astronomer who worked at the Jodrell Bank Observatory and later became a professor of physical electronics. His widely publicized 1963 account of a glowing sphere passing down an aircraft aisle became one of the most cited ball lightning reports.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: An 18th-century Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who was killed while experimenting with atmospheric electricity in 1753. His death was long popularly depicted as caused by a ball of lightning, cementing the phenomenon's image as deadly, even though investigation showed it was an ordinary lightning strike from an ungrounded conductor.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A short-lived paralysis or loss of sensation in a limb caused by a nearby lightning or ball lightning strike, distinct from longer-lasting nerve damage or psychological trauma.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: A 19th-century French physician regarded as the founder of modern neurology, based at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris, and a teacher of Sigmund Freud. He studied a patient's account of a ball lightning encounter to distinguish short-term shock paralysis from lasting psychological trauma.

entries.name: soil strike theory
aliases: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: The idea that ball lightning can form when a lightning strike hits soil, vaporizing minerals in the ground into a glowing ball of hot gas and burning particles. The theory is supported in the piece by a 2012 case where a camera's spectrum of a ball lightning event showed the chemical signatures of soil elements like iron, calcium, and silicon.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.senseHere: A proposed collaborative European research program on the physics of lightning, cited here as the forum where about 30 researchers agreed that ball lightning is a real, if poorly documented, phenomenon.
